commits.author: asartran
commits.message:
[grug] Read precomputed fa4_bounds in the AMD Pallas flash kernel (#10217)

Let the AMD Pallas flash attention kernel (`gpu_pallas_triton_flash`)
accept masks that carry precomputed `fa4_bounds`. Before this change it
rejected them, so `moe_hero_ep`, `moe_hero_fsdp` and `fast_track` could
not run on AMD GPUs with this kernel.

`fa4_bounds` is a pair of per-query arrays: the lowest key position each
query may attend to, and a flag for whether the query is a real token or
padding. These three models run all their layers in one `lax.scan`, and
different layers use different (long or short) sliding windows. The
window size is a static field of `AttentionMask`, so the scan body
cannot change it from layer to layer. The models instead precompute one
set of bounds per window size and pick one per layer
(`experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py:1338-1359`). The kernel now uses
those bounds as each query's key lower bound, as `gpu_fa4_cute` already
does.

Outputs match the segment-ID path except on padding rows. A padding
query attends only to itself, and the loss masks those rows.

The kernel does not check the bounds. After each padding row's bound is
set to its own position, the bounds must never decrease from one query
to the next and must not exceed each query's position.
`fa4_cute_segment_bounds` produces bounds like this when each segment ID
occupies one contiguous run. The dK/dV pass relies on that ordering, so
bounds that break it give wrong key and value gradients without raising
an error. The module docstring and the comment on
`AttentionMask.fa4_bounds` state this requirement.

The tests check the `moe_hero_ep` pattern against the reference
implementation on a 2x2 data/model mesh, with bounds computed outside a
`lax.scan`, sharded over the batch, and selected per layer with
`jnp.where`. A GPU-only test is the only one that compiles the default
tile sizes a training run uses; it runs bfloat16 at 4096 tokens with a
2048 window, through precomputed bounds as `moe_hero_ep` passes them. CI
runs on CPU, so it skips this test.

Part of #9812.

commits.author: yonromai
commits.message:
[iris] Bound federation peer RPCs with a 60-second default (#10857)

Give federation peer RPCs a 60-second default deadline, preserving explicit limits. Status-sync and job-cancel RPCs share a loop with job delivery. An RPC timeout lets that loop resume; sync timeouts preserve the cursor for retry.

The [November 2 incident](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/916) exposed an unbounded sync wait. Its initiating cause remains unknown.

All 38 tests in `test_federation.py`, formatting checks and type checks passed.

commits.author: asartran
commits.message:
[experiments] Add opt-in collective-overlap flags for multi-node AMD runs (#10673)

Jobs launched through `experiments/amd/hpcfund/run_gpu.sh` can now pass
`--overlap-collectives` to get five XLA flags that overlap collectives
with compute. On two MI350X nodes this cuts the June Snowball step by
13%, without model code changes. Jobs that don't pass the option are
unchanged.

With data parallelism across nodes, each node holds a full copy of the
model, and each layer's expert-weight gradients are summed across the
nodes by an all-reduce over the network. XLA issues that all-reduce
inside the backward pass's loop over layers and, by default, runs it
with nothing to overlap it, so the GPUs wait for the network. On two
MI355X nodes about a quarter of the profiled step was this exposed
all-reduce.

With `--overlap-collectives` before the script, the wrapper adds: the
latency-hiding scheduler, up to 4 collectives in flight at once (XLA's
default is 1), pipelined all-reduce (XLA moves each loop iteration's
all-reduce into the next iteration, where compute can hide it),
while-loop double buffering, and starting each collective as soon as its
inputs are ready. Caller `XLA_FLAGS` still override any of them. The
flags are opt-in because of the correctness caveat below: they change
only scheduling, but more than one collective in flight has corrupted
training elsewhere.

June Snowball (`synthetic_benchmark.py --size full`), EP8 inside each
node and data parallelism across nodes (`--expert-axis 8 --replica-axis
2`), 8 sequences of 4,096 tokens per GPU, `--moe-impl ring_filtered
--pooled-transport-capacity-factor 1.1 --attention
gpu_pallas_triton_flash --remat-mode save_moe`, median step of steps
2-19:

| Setup | Before | After | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2x MI350X nodes, HPC Fund, this wrapper and venv | 1.975-1.982 s |
1.715-1.717 s | -13% |
| 1x MI350X node, all nine flags of the ablation below | 1.529-1.534 s |
1.526-1.529 s | none |
| 2x MI355X nodes, Vultr, TheRock 7.14 container, main `666cf38f51` |
1.955-1.971 s | 1.709-1.736 s | -12% |

In both two-node MI350X jobs, the second run without the flags was
slower on every step (2.134 s and 3.026 s); the cause is unknown, and
the table uses the first run of each job. Peak memory rises by at most 1
GiB.

A leave-one-out ablation on two MI355X nodes picked the five flags:
starting from nine flags (five runs, 1.707-1.740 s, median 1.725 s), it
removed one at a time, one run each.

| Flag removed | Step | Change |
|---|---|---|
| latency-hiding scheduler | 2.065 s | +20% |
| overlap limit 4 | 1.964 s | +14% |
| start collectives as early as possible | 1.793 s | +3.9% |
| pipelined all-reduce | 1.768 s | +2.5% |
| while-loop double buffering | 1.752 s | +1.6% |
| pipelined all-gather | 1.729 s | none |
| pipelined reduce-scatter | 1.719 s | none |
| 8 GiB all-gather and reduce-scatter combine thresholds | 1.715 s |
none |

The last three are dropped. With the overlap limit at 1, the remaining
flags give no gain (1.964 s, the same as no flags).

On GB200, more than one collective in flight silently corrupted training
with Grug's ragged all-to-all transport and the layer-carry offload, so
the NVIDIA EP hero forces the limit to 1. Here, two runs with the five
flags and two without differ in per-step loss by at most 2.7e-4 and in
capacity-drop rate (the share of tokens dropped because their expert's
buffer is full) by at most 0.4 points; the two runs without the flags
already differ from each other by 1.5e-4 and 0.3 points. These runs use
synthetic tokens and an untrained router, which detect such races
poorly. Parity from a trained-router checkpoint has not been checked;
the README says to check it before a long run, or to set the overlap
limit to 1 in `XLA_FLAGS` to rule the race out at the cost of the gain.

Limits, also recorded in the README: the flags were measured only with
replica data parallelism on two nodes, not cross-node FSDP or EP16. With
the HPC Fund venv, 4 of 17 runs with the flags crashed while shutting
down after their last step (`double free or corruption` as
`jax.distributed` disconnects, or a segfault), and one more segfaulted
during compilation, against 0 of 6 runs without them. Output up to the
crash is complete, but Slurm marks the step failed. All 22 flagged runs
in the MI355X container exited cleanly.

Part of #9812.

commits.author: mcwitt
commits.message:
[grug] Make FA4 zigzag context sharding configurable (#10610)

Add `GrugModelConfig.attention_context_layout`, passed through
`attention()` to the FA4 wrappers, so a run can turn off the zigzag
query swap from #10170. `"zigzag"` stays the default, so 262K and every
other context-parallel caller is unchanged. `"contiguous"` makes one
kernel call per shard on its own query rows at offset `shard_index *
local_len`, with no query split and no `ppermute`, the same code path as
before #10170.

Zigzag pays off at 262K (see #10170 for the benchmarks) but slightly
slows 65K, so the hero README says to keep `"zigzag"` at 262K and set
`"contiguous"` at 65K, one `HERO_MODEL` line in `heuristic.py`.

The #10170 CPU position test now runs under both layouts and checks that
every query row reaches the kernel at its global position. The GPU
parity test for sequence-sharded queries (forward and gradients against
reference attention) now also runs under both layouts. An unknown layout
value raises `ValueError` at the FA4 entry point.

commits.author: muchanem
commits.message:
[taskforge] Add triage: structural checks and a surface for expansion (#10296)

Add triage as a deterministic preflight. `stage20_triage.checks` holds the proposal checks that read what `parse` leaves open, each reporting PASS, FAIL or SKIP: the required sections have content (fatal), and the grader section matches the declared verification, every research item states a purpose and the build plan names every declared resource (advisory). `stage20_triage.preflight.preflight(proposal)` runs them and rejects a fatal failure or a null proposal with the reason, accepts anything else, and makes no model call. Header validity is `parse`'s job: it also refuses a resource path outside the build root and a repeated build name. Whether the host can provide the machine is the build's check. `verdict.py` holds the `Verdict` record and `TriageDecision`, whose REPAIR value and `author_state` field are the surface a consumer's triage may use.

The preflight is the default, and the package has no model review: the README describes a panel with repair and a bounded review with obligations as designs a consumer could add, which experiments found not to be meaningful predictors of downstream quality. `StageCoordinator` still triages with `verdict.accept` here; #10298 moves it onto the preflight's verdict.

Builds on #10295; #10297 builds on it.

commits.author: muchanem
commits.message:
[taskforge] Define typed JSON task proposals and resumable sources (#10295)

Define typed task proposals with a source identity, environment and verification requirements, research and build plans, and a Markdown body stored inside JSON. Parsing checks the required sections, machine constraints and research citations; canonical serialization gives each proposal a stable content digest.

Generation uses a JSON schema derived from the proposal dataclasses. This replaces the YAML front-matter parser and document regex while retaining semantic validation and rejecting duplicate keys. Existing YAML artifacts require their original consumer or explicit conversion; their serialized digests change under JSON.

The proposal source plans a set of candidate tasks before writing each proposal independently. Callers can persist that plan and resume an individual proposal without regenerating its siblings. Builds on #10294; #10296 adds deterministic triage.

The repository pre-commit gate, 399 offline Taskforge and experiment tests, and the package type check pass.

commits.author: muchanem
commits.message:
[taskforge] Add TaskSpec assembly, lowering, controls and verdicts (#10294)

The Taskforge build stage produces a task as builder outputs (an instruction, files, an answer and a grader program), and validation runs it under RolloutEngine on whichever host it is on. This adds the `spec` package that turns those outputs into a `TaskSpec` and lowers it for the host.

`spec.draft.assemble` builds the semantic `TaskSpec` and refuses a task that would leak or corrupt its grading: private grader content the solver can read, or an agent-visible file under the grader's `/tests` and `/logs/verifier` roots, which grading stages after the grader's own files. `spec.draft.lower` builds the `TaskRolloutSpec` RolloutEngine runs under its shell harness (`draft.rollout_engine`) and is the one place that chooses each machine's backend. A machine on the grader base image moves to the local backend's CPython only when nothing staged or written on it lies under a system directory that backend cannot write: all of them for a read-only factory, only `/sys` and the resolver's directory for the copy-on-write factory Taskforge builds on Iris. Package machines take PyPI requirements one per entry, and an entry carrying a uv requirements-file option is refused.

`spec.controls` defines the fixed controls a task's control set must hold (a reference, an acceptance and a shortcut control) and turns a candidate's files and reply into the turns a replay serves. `spec.verdict` reads and writes the per-check verdict a grader program reports. `child_process` stops a child process group, for the loader and build children of the later stages.

Builds on #10293. The shared modules are complete here, and #10295 starts the stages. The RolloutEngine tests of `llm.rollout_model`, the ShellSim fixture images and the sandbox factories' two manual machine tests need `spec.draft`, so they land here.

commits.author: muchanem
commits.message:
[taskforge] Add machine factories, task images and the image builder (#10293)

Taskforge needs explicit machine backends and a way to build custom task images. Add the shared `sandbox` package.

`machine_factories(backends, controller_url)` constructs exactly the selected shellbox backends and raises when requested Docker or local sandbox support is unavailable. ShellSim-only runs do not probe either. `task_refusals` checks a task's machine requirements before starting a trial.

`IrisImageBuilder` builds a custom image in one Iris CPU job, pushes it in a separate job, and returns a digest-pinned reference after registry readback. Both jobs disable inherited-secret forwarding and receive the submitter's CoreWeave storage credentials for output archives. Only the push job receives registry authentication. Bootstrap and readback errors are classified as infrastructure failures. Build contexts reuse TaskCompendium's validation and are size-checked before file contents are read.

Builds on #10292; #10294 builds on this. The full repository pre-commit gate, 255 offline Taskforge and experiment tests, and the package type check pass. These changes have not been tested with a live build-to-pull run.

commits.author: mcwitt
commits.message:
[grug] Let the hero launcher run context parallelism (#10618)

The hero's 262K context extension needs context parallelism, and CP4
with row balancing is a throughput option at 65K, but the production
hero launcher (`launch_scaling_ladder.py`, d6144) did not support it: it
fixed the expert axis at all 64 GPUs of a rack and had no context axis.
Only `launch_diagnostics.py` could run CP. The launcher now can:

- `hero_recipe.py` adds the checked-in constants `HERO_CONTEXT_AXIS_SIZE
= 1` and `HERO_BALANCE_ATTENTION_ROWS = False` (#10121's row balancing),
so a deploy that turns on CP sets each with one line.
- At CP > 1 each rack's 64 GPUs (`HERO_RACK_GPUS`, formerly
`HERO_EP_EXPERT_AXIS_SIZE`) form 64 / CP expert shards, and the Levanter
trainer mesh counts only batch shards, as `launch_diagnostics.py`
already did.
- The eval batch is one sequence per batch shard, so each GPU on the
dropless eval mesh holds max_seq_len / CP tokens per eval batch: 704
sequences on the 11-rack hero at CP1, 176 at CP4.
- All three hero launchers share one launch-time check that the batch,
`max_seq_len` and the expert bank split over the layout. Its waves check
now applies only to the pooled-wave transport, the one that splits local
experts into waves. `launch_diagnostics.py` defaults its context axis
and row balancing to the hero constants.
- Levanter's `compact_grug_mesh_shape` is public, since the shared check
sizes the mesh with it.
- The loader logs each source's start offset at a context switch.

The running hero is unchanged: its full built config at 65K CP1
(trainer, mesh, eval, model, optimizer) has the same repr as on `main`,
and tests pin the CP1 and CP4 layouts.

Part of #8435

[rolloutengine] Document length-cut tool calls and unrendered generation-limit prompts (#9839)

Document two model-adapter rules that `main` implements but does not
state, and test the behaviour behind them.

Machine preparation and the shell tool contract, the exports this PR
originally added, are now public on `main` in another form. #10203
exported `rolloutengine.machines.task_machine(task, factory, runtime, *,
cleanup_timeout)`. The shell tool contract lives in

them only when no turn of the conversation completed.

generation-limit paragraph.
- `test_rollout.py`: a length-cut tool call is graded without being
executed; `task_machine` raises a close failure after a clean body;
`task_machine` closes its machine when setup fails.

commits.author: ravwojdyla-agent
commits.message:
[datakit] Release the shared Zephyr pool after its last stage (#10067)

Release the shared Zephyr pool when its last stage succeeds, so idle
shared workers stop holding hosts needed by dedicated pools.
`run_reference_steps` runs normalization before starting the shared
pool; a watcher thread calls `ZephyrContext.shutdown()` after every step
in `DatakitSteps.shared_pool_steps` succeeds. `ZephyrDatakitSteps` and
`DecontaminationSteps` each list the stages that receive the shared
context. If the watcher's status check raises, the run fails with that
error. All three ferries use this path through `run_reference_ferry`, as
does `reference_pipeline.py --target all`. The shared pool uses
`_IdleWorkerPolicy.RETAIN`, so it previously kept every acquired worker
until the DAG ended: up to 512 workers (2 CPU / 16 GiB each) on v5e
hosts, while the embed, quality, fuzzy-cluster, and store pools waited
for hosts.

Reduce the tier-1 store worker from 4 CPU / 32 GiB RAM / 64 GiB disk to
2 CPU / 8 GiB RAM / 16 GiB disk. A store task with one normalized shard
peaks below 2 GiB RAM and spills below 1 GiB. On 2026-10-12, the old
shape received 1 of 106 workers; the new shape received 12 workers in 1
minute.

On the fixed code, tier 1 (`/rav/iris-run-job-20261012-153556`)
succeeded in 56 minutes. Tier 3 (`/rav/iris-run-job-20261012-153605`)
succeeded, and its shared pool stopped at 19:30 UTC after fuzzy dedup.
Tier 3 took 5h47m, exceeding the 20,700-second CI wait. On a busy
cluster, the shared pool received only 275 of its 512 workers, and
tokenization took 2h37m, compared with 37 minutes on 2026-10-05.

The tier-3 fuzzy-cluster workers drop from 16 CPU / 128 GiB / 64 GiB
disk to 8 CPU / 64 GiB / 32 GiB, with 64 instead of 32 workers, so the
task count stays at 512. Only one of the larger workers fits on a v5e
host. On 2026-10-13 the verify workers waited 3h46m for hosts, and the
tier-3 ferry took 7h30m. At 16 tasks per worker, cluster text peaked at
66 GiB and verify at 26 GiB.

The three tiers passed in CI on this branch. Tier 1 took 56 minutes, and
tier 2 took 1h51m. Tier 3 (`/runner/iris-run-job-20261013-165715`) took
2h25m, with 36 minutes for fuzzy verification. This is much less than
the 20,700-second CI wait.

The tier concurrency groups now include `github.ref`, so a run started
on a branch and the scheduled run on main do not cancel each other.

Fixes https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10047. Part of
https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10059.

commits.author: mcwitt
commits.message:
[grug] Switch the hero to 65K context at permanent step 372000 (#10820)

The hero trains at 65,536-token context from permanent step-372000 of `hero-gradclip-step356k`, on the same CP1 × EP64 mesh as at 16K, with qk_mult 1.66 and receiver capacity factor 1.5 (up from 1.15). Each rack keeps 4,194,304 tokens per update, so the 11-rack batch is 704 sequences. The 16K phase is appended to the hero's context history with the parent's cumulative FLOPs at step 372000, and the launch record names the child run, handoff checkpoint and W&B fork point. That leaves 18,251 steps (4.7%, 0.84T tokens) at 65K.

`HERO_FLOPS_BASELINE_TOTAL` is the parent's `throughput/total_gflops` × 1e9 projected to W&B `_step` 371999: the parent adds the same FLOPs every 16K step, and projecting from `_step` 359999 matches the logged total at 369975 to 8e-13. The logged value is checked against it before launch.

On one GB200 rack at 65K, CP1 with capacity factor 1.5 ran at 15.397 s/step with drop fraction 9.80e-4 and peak HBM 128.4 GiB, against 14.699 s, 2.41e-3 and 127.6 GiB for CP4 × EP16, over 500 steps each; its dropless eval completes. CP1 at capacity factor 1.0 drops 1.9% of assignments. qk_mult 1.66 is 1.3 × (0.1 ln(65536/4096) + 1). The one-rack test of this branch ([`tok350-deploy65k-c1-01`](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/tok350-deploy65k-c1-01)), restored from step-360000, ran 60 steps at 15.571 s/step median with drop fraction 8.29e-4 and peak HBM 127.9 GiB; three dropless evals completed (Paloma macro loss 1.995–1.998) with no OOM or retry. Its step is 1.1% slower than the earlier arm's; this branch includes the gradient clipping of #10783, which that arm predated. A 100-step rehearsal from step-366000 ran at 15.518 s/step median with peak HBM 127.9 GiB through two checkpoint saves.

Part of #8435; tracked in #10821.

[datakit] Shuffle MinHash LSH buckets as uint64 keys (#10106)

Shuffle MinHash LSH buckets through the connected-components group_by as
Python ints instead of decimal strings. `_emit_bucket_records` casts
each batch's `buckets` column to `list<uint64>` with pyarrow and yields
the ints; `CCInput.bucket` and the CC reducer and combiner annotations
become `int`. The bucket is only a routing key for that group_by. CC
never writes it to its link or node files, so nothing persisted changes.

`fuzzy_minhash.py` is untouched: on-disk MinHash attrs stay
`list<string>`, `MINHASH_ATTR_DATA_VERSION` stays 3 and
`FUZZY_DUPS_ATTR_DATA_VERSION` is unchanged. No step hash, output path
or hero-manifest entry moves, and the final fuzzy-dup output is
identical to main. String-encoded and `list<uint64>` attrs canonicalize
to the same int key, so mixed sources still link, as they did through
`str(b)` on main. A bucket string that does not parse as uint64 now
fails the job with `ArrowInvalid`; on main it became a key that matched
only the same malformed string. Arrow's parser also accepts forms such
as `0x10` and `007`, which the MinHash writer never emits.

This is phase 1. Writing `list<uint64>` attrs on disk, with the matching
`MINHASH_ATTR_DATA_VERSION` bump, is deferred until the planned MinHash
rerun, since it invalidates cached attrs.
